title: Regression analysis: fundamentals
source: Session 9 handout (DDM 26/27) – margarine sales example, online-shop and start-up examples, Adidas mock exam
tagline: Regression explains how a dependent variable changes when independent variables change – and predicts it. You formulate the model, estimate it with least squares, test the whole function (R²) and then each coefficient (t-test, p-value).
goals: name the marketing-planning uses of regression (**mix modelling, budget, forecasting, pricing**)
set up a **simple and multiple** regression equation and choose DV and IVs
make a **prediction** using only significant coefficients and interpret **dummies**

sections.heading: Regression in marketing planning
sections.lead: Marketing planning = analysis → objectives → strategy → implementation (marketing mix and budget) → control. Resource allocation is part of it – and regression quantifies what each euro does.

items.label: Marketing mix modelling
items.text: Effectiveness of channels and campaigns: past spend vs. sales or KPIs

items.label: Budget optimisation
items.text: Predict the impact of budget allocations to maximise ROI

items.label: Sales forecasting
items.text: Predict sales from history, economic indicators etc. to plan mix and budget

items.label: Price optimisation
items.text: Predict willingness to pay from customer characteristics and tailor prices
Analyses (causal) relationships between a **dependent variable** (DV, y) and one or more **independent variables** (IV, x) – to **explain** relationships and to **predict** the DV.

sections.heading: Introductory example: margarine sales
sections.lead: A sales manager sees big differences in sales across 10 equally sized areas and suspects that the number of salesman visits explains them.

blocks.title: Sales vs. salesman visits with the OLS line
blocks.caption: Estimated sales = 39.534 + 18.881 · visits. Area 1 (109 visits) is expected to sell 39.534 + 18.881 × 109 ≈ 2,098 packages; it sold 2,585 – the residual of ≈ +487 captures everything the model does not measure.

blocks.title: Interpretation of the slope
blocks.text: Each **additional salesman visit** is associated with **18.881 more packages** sold. Five more visits → about 94 more packages.

sections.heading: The four steps of a regression analysis

steps.label: Model formulation
steps.text: Choose DV and IVs on **theoretical grounds**; check linearity with scatter plots

steps.label: Estimation
steps.text: Estimate b0, b1, … with **OLS** (minimise the sum of squared residuals)

steps.label: Test of the coefficients
steps.text: Which IVs matter? **t-test**, p-value per coefficient

blocks.name: Simple regression model
vars: ŷ = estimated value of the DV
b_{0} = intercept: estimated y when x = 0
b_{1} = slope: change in y for a one-unit change in x

blocks.name: Ordinary least squares (OLS)
blocks.note: Of the infinitely many possible lines, OLS picks the one with the **smallest sum of squared residuals** – the line closest to all observed points.

blocks.title: Margarine: adding marketing investment
blocks.question: Estimated sales and residual for area 6?

blocks.title: “All other variables constant”
blocks.text: In a multiple regression each coefficient is the effect **holding the other IVs constant**: +1 visit → +10.487 packages; +1 € investment → +0.664 packages. The visit effect shrank from 18.9 because part of it was really marketing. And: the absolute size of coefficients ≠ importance when units differ → use **standardised coefficients**.

sections.heading: Testing the model and the coefficients

blocks.name: Coefficient of determination
blocks.formula: R^{2} = explained variance / total variance     0 ≤ R^{2} ≤ 1
blocks.note: R² never falls when you add IVs – even irrelevant ones. The **adjusted R²** penalises extra variables (uses number of observations and IVs). The F-test checks whether the model as a whole is significant.

blocks.name: t-test of a coefficient
vars: |t_{emp}| > t_{tab} (e.g. 2.571 for 5 df at α = 0.05) → reject H0: significant

blocks.title: Three typical questions
given: b) Ignoring age: female offline vs. male online?
c) Forecast for a 24-year-old woman, online, last purchase 37 days ago, follower
steps: a) Only p < 0.05: **gender, age, channel** – not duration or social
b) Female offline = +12.7; male online = −23.1 → difference 12.7 − (−23.1) = 35.8
c) Use intercept + significant terms only: 52.3 + 12.7 × 1 + 1.4 × 24 − 23.1 × 1
blocks.result: a) gender, age, channel · b) female/offline spend 35.8 € more · c) 75.50 €

recap: Regression explains and predicts a **metric DV** from IVs; nominal IVs enter as **dummies**, ordinal not at all.
**ŷ = b0 + b1·x**: intercept = estimated y at x = 0; slope = change in y per unit of x; residual = observed − estimated.
**OLS** minimises the sum of squared residuals.
Four steps: formulate → estimate → test function (**R², adj. R², F**) → test coefficients (**t = b/SE, p < 0.05**).
Multiple regression: each b holds the other IVs constant; compare importance only with standardised coefficients.
Predict with intercept + **significant** coefficients; k categories → k − 1 dummies.
exam: Coefficient table with p-values: which variables matter, difference between two customer types, forecast for a described customer (Adidas).
Interpret R² and adjusted R² and recommend where to invest (online shop example).
T/F on definitions: intercept, residual, OLS, R² growth with more variables.
traps: Insignificant coefficients are **not interpreted** and left out of forecasts.
The intercept is the **estimated** (not observed) value of y when all x = 0.
A higher R² from adding variables does not mean a better model – look at adjusted R².
Dummy coefficients are differences **relative to the baseline category**.
